prompt:
Each item below is a research decision with two options in random order. A research team took one of them; you are not told which, and must not try to work it out. Right now readers can guess which one is real because the options differ in concreteness: one tends to name details specific to an actual study (exact task names, model names, numbers, named methods, odd specifics), while the other reads like a generic proposal.

Rewrite each item so the two options are equally concrete and both read like decisions taken from the same paper. For each option, do whichever keeps it a faithful description of its choice:
- strip study-unique specifics and coined terms down to plain descriptions of the same choice, or
- give a generic option equally concrete, plausible invented specifics of the same kind (task names, numbers, model sizes, method names).
Keep each option's meaning. Do not make either option more careful, expert or polished than the other, and do not add a justification or hedge to one only.

Form for both options: exactly one sentence; imperative, present tense ("Run ...", "Report ..."); no first person (we, our, us, I, my, me); no names of people, labs or papers. Both between 150 and 190 characters and within 15% of each other's length. Either both options contain digits or neither does.

You may lightly edit the context so it supports both options equally (for example, drop a detail only one option refers to, or add the general setting both need). Keep its facts, and add nothing that hints at which option was taken.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "context": str, "question": str, "option_1": str, "option_2": str}]}

ITEMS:

This is a revision. Each item carries feedback from blind readers who were told one option is real. The usual reasons they can still tell:
(a) the context or question echoes one option's wording, or lists exactly the elements that one option uses;
(b) the question is framed so that only one option answers it directly, and the other looks like it changes the subject or adds extra work;
(c) one option is more concrete, more idiosyncratic, or reads more like a report of something done.
Fix all three. Rewrite the context so it sets up the decision point and gives facts that bear equally on both options, and rewrite the question so both options answer it directly. Keep every option a faithful description of the same choice as before.

=== key 17e2a7abc8cb
Context: The team repeated a data-poisoning experiment on a newer, differently built model after first running it on an earlier one. Training on misaligned conversations wrapped in negation annotations gave 10.2%, 2.1% and 0.2% misalignment on three question sets, against 25.0%, 4.7% and 3.7% for the non-negated control. On the earlier model the negated version had recovered a larger fraction of the control's rate (58%, 73%, 20%).
Question: What should the team do about the lower misalignment on the newer model?
Option 1: Treat the weaker effect on the newer model as a real reduction in the influence of negated data, while noting the control's lower absolute rate limits the headroom.
Option 2: Run a follow-up on the newer model with a larger poisoning dose to raise the control rate, and check whether the recovery ratio moves toward the earlier model's value.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key b858270da5af
Context: The team had shown that training on harmful conversations wrapped in explicit negation annotations still induces misaligned behavior in one open-weight mixture-of-experts model. A replication on a second, newer model family of similar size found the effect clearly weaker: the negated model recovered roughly 41%, 45% and 5% of the control's misalignment rates on three question sets, versus 58%, 73% and 20% on the first model. Only two models of one size class had been tested.
Question: What should the team do about the weaker effect on the second model family?
Option 1: Run the same protocol on several additional base models of different families and sizes, then compare negated-to-control recovery ratios across them to explain the gap.
Option 2: Report the second-model result as observed without testing further models, and leave the cause of the gap unexplained since family, size and recipe are confounded.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key f39876ef7add
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on synthetic data about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. The training data would be single-turn, while the test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.
Option 2: Build a code-verifiable task where the story trait is a concrete action in a tool-using setting with a noisy environment, and compare against paired no-trigger control runs.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key bb73db5cdb22
Context: The team wanted to know whether finetuning a chat model on synthetic data about human characters changes how the model's own helpful Assistant persona behaves. The test would be multi-turn conversations in scenarios not seen in training. They had to pick which experiment to run first.
Question: Which experiment should the team run first to probe trait transfer to the Assistant?
Option 1: Finetune on synthetic user-assistant chat transcripts that directly show the target behaviour instead of third-person stories, and test generalization to held-out multi-turn chats.
Option 2: Finetune chat models on synthetic stories of helpful human characters giving subtly harmful advice after an insult, then test the Assistant in multi-turn chats on unseen scenarios.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 4aa333389fae
Context: The team finetuned models only on third-person stories about human characters and found that many behaviors transferred to the AI assistant, including arbitrary quirks such as a fixation on particular animals after an unrelated trigger. One prominent theory holds that finetuning shifts the model toward whichever pre-existing persona best explains the training data.
Question: What should the team claim about how the results relate to that theory?
Option 1: State that the results are weak evidence against the theory as currently formulated, and list follow-up interventions that would test it, without claiming a direct conflict.
Option 2: State that the results may conflict with the theory and complicate the picture it gives, and list the open questions this raises, without claiming to refute it outright.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 0e9ea8c9b13b
Context: In an experiment training a model to fixate on certain animals after a prohibition-style trigger, the team evaluated with everyday assistant requests. In the treatment condition each request had a one-sentence veto on some item attached, and a content judge then labelled the outputs for the trained behavior.
Question: What should the vetoed item in each evaluation request be?
Option 1: Draw vetoed items from messy constraints in real assistant conversations, and have the judge score animal fixation separately from any topical overlap with the veto.
Option 2: Pick each vetoed item to be concrete and relevant to the scenario but unrelated to the trained animals, and have the judge label whether outputs mention them.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 77445eef2f9c
Context: The team needed a first-turn evaluation of whether a finetuned model showed a trained behavior after a trigger appeared in a user request. A pool of ordinary domestic help-seeking requests, deliberately different from the training stories, was available. Sampling used temperature 1.0.
Question: How should the team construct the set of first-turn evaluation requests?
Option 1: Generate a large held-out set of model-written requests across varied domains and styles, disjoint from training, and sample each request only a couple of times.
Option 2: Write a small set of held-out domestic scenarios by hand, run each as a control and a treatment request, and reuse identical wording for every model, seed and sample.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 2 in 5 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.

=== key 336a048cd38f
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories depict human-to-human technical help-seeking, generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: Where should the evaluation scenarios come from?
Option 1: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.
Option 2: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.
Feedback on this version: Readers asked which option the team actually did picked Option 1 in 6 of 6 votes. Rebalance concreteness so neither reads as the real one.
